patch.value: Executable acceptance criteria: every criterion carries a machine-checkable predicate and a recorded verdict, so done is computed rather than asserted

Acceptance criteria are the field the whole lifecycle turns on and they are free prose joined by semicolons. Nothing can evaluate them, so closing an item is an assertion by whoever closed it, and the close-time completeness work can only check that certain fields are non-empty, never that the criteria hold. Linked tests are the closest existing mechanism, but they attach to the item rather than to a criterion, so a green test run does not say which criterion it satisfied and a partially met set of criteria is indistinguishable from a fully met one. The proposal is to let each criterion optionally declare how it is checked, with the check being any of a linked test command, a query over workspace state, a file or documentation predicate, or an explicit human sign-off, and to record the outcome of each check as a verdict with a timestamp, an author and the evidence that produced it. Prose-only criteria remain valid and unevaluated, so nothing existing breaks and adoption is incremental. Two consequences make this worth more than its size: strict close validation becomes able to require that every criterion has a passing verdict rather than that the field is non-empty, and any external grader, including a training environment, can read the verdict set as its score without knowing anything about the item's domain.

A criterion may declare a check of at least the linked-test, workspace-query, artifact-predicate and human-signoff kinds, and criteria without a check remain valid; running the checks for an item produces a per-criterion verdict recording pass, fail or not-evaluated, with timestamp, author and the evidence, and the verdicts are stored on the item and appended to history; close validation can be configured to require passing verdicts for every criterion, and the default is unchanged so existing workspaces are unaffected; the verdict set is readable as a bounded projection cheap enough for an agent loop and reachable through the SDK; a criterion's check is re-runnable at any later point and re-running is idempotent; the existing prose criteria corpus is untouched and no migration is required

value.text:
Structural prerequisite recorded 2026-07-30 (evening). Acceptance criteria are stored and returned as a single semicolon-delimited scalar string, not as a collection. Verified on disk and through the read path: the toon field is one quoted string, pm get returns a string of 756 characters on the item I checked, repeated --ac flags accumulate by joining with a semicolon and a space, and --add-ac rejects a criterion that contains a semicolon because that character is the separator. The largest live example carries 195 criteria in one field.

That means a criterion has no addressable identity today. It cannot be referenced, it cannot carry a per-criterion state, and it cannot be linked to the test that proves it, because there is nothing to link to. Every one of this item's promises depends on that: a machine-checkable predicate has to attach to something, and a criterion that exists only as a substring of a scalar cannot be an attachment point.

So the first tranche of this item is a representation change, not a predicate language: criteria become an ordered collection of records with stable identity, each able to carry text, an optional predicate, and a verification state, with the existing semicolon-joined form preserved as the rendered projection so no consumer breaks and no history entry becomes unreadable. The separator restriction disappears as a consequence rather than as a fix, and the current rejection of a semicolon inside a criterion becomes the regression test that proves the representation actually changed.

Two adjacent facts to reuse rather than rediscover. The validate surface already counts criteria, so a count is derivable from the scalar today and any migration must keep that count identical. And an item with criteria but no linked test is exactly the population this item exists to shrink, which makes the criterion-to-test edge the first useful predicate to ship once identity exists.
